The explanation could hold water, but that only demonstrates plausibility, not truth. Seems that a router that previously terminated copper interfaces was switched to terminate fiber. That alone doesn't really tell us much without knowing whether this is really all that happened or if it's shorthand for a bigger move at a higher level in the protocol stack. For example you might "just" have changed copper Cat6 ports to fiber/SFP but still be doing GigEthernet and I rather doubt that a move that simple could make a router misbehave. Moving up the stack this get more interesting. For example they might have moved from a copper star topology to a fiber ring, and rings need care or else chaos ensues. Similarly Ethernet gets pissy if there are loops but the spanning tree protocols need very careful usage. I assume since the word router was used that Ethernet was fine and we are in layer 3. An interface switch could have triggered recalculation or reannouncement of routes, for example by erroneously configured routing protocols. eg the Arkansas router announces it is the best hop for traffic to reach Chicago, gets swamped with traffic from Dallas, NY, etc, and falls over. (Yes, the tools provide guardrails. Who knows if they were enabled?) However, and esp because Duffy is pointing at L3Harris, I suspect they installed (or perhaps removed) a Juniper TDM to Ethernet converter module (eg DS3 SmartSFP from that vendor) and something went bad. These modules are supposed to encap TDM into Ethernet but they don't (iirc) have any semantic awareness of a telephone call, so if they were to be hit by, say, a storm of TDM circuit messages (call setups, say) they might just pass them on, not rate limit them like a true telco packet switch would. It might be pure coincidence that an AI system was hooked up to the FAA system the week before. Bottom line: could be bad luck, could be basic screw up, we won't know for years.

WPA2 was formally verified at the protocol level, but the formal specification -- while reviewed by multiple humans -- was flawed, which directly led to the KRACK attack. I've been having a seamless dual-boot experience with Windows 11 and Linux Mint Debian Edition, LMDE7. As a preface to those Mint instructions, in Windows Disk Management I shrink the main Windows partition by about 20GB to 50GB, this creates some new "unallocated space" immediately following the normal Windows C: volume. Then create a "New Simple Volume" in that unallocated space, but do not assign a drive letter and do not format. This will be the sole Linux partition, no /swap, no /usr, none of that monkey business when you are not replacing Windows , merely adding Linux as an option to a "virtually unchanged" Windows PC. You want Linux to occupy a single partition just like Windows does. At the Command prompt in Windows Diskpart, next select the target HDD or SSD, then select the target Linux partition on that drive, and "SET ID=4F68BCE3-E8CD-4DB1-96E7-FBCAF984B709 which is the designator for Linux Root. Also in Diskpart you can select the EFI volume and assign an alphabetical letter to the EFI volume so you can see the hidden folders and back up the Windows-specific \EFI\Boot\bootx64.efi file contained within. Manipulating the "hidden" EFI files can only be done at the Command prompt (not the GUI) after assigning a drive letter like this, and after you reboot, that drive letter will be removed automatically and no more access to EFI unless you reassign a drive letter again in CMD. Then boot to the LMDE7 USB drive so you can install Linux to the unformatted partition. In the Mint install wizard you will have to choose the "Manual" partitioning & formatting option, which opens up infinite possibilities, but this simple dual-boot arrangement only takes a couple distinct settings. In the displayed list of partitions, select that unformatted volume as "root", indicated by the single slash "/", and choose to format it using ext2, ext3, or ext4. Then in the small fat32 boot partition (where the Windows boot files are already residing in the "hidden" \EFI\Microsoft\ folder), Do Not format this partition, but select it as the ideal location for the Linux boot files, and designate it as "/EFI/Boot". That's it. After completion, Linux will be completely independent from Windows. In the EFI boot volume there will be a new \EFI\debian\ folder alongside the \EFI\Microsoft\ folder. The only change to any Microsoft files (and it's a "big" one) is within the \EFI\Boot\ folder which is a common folder to all the OS's on that SSD. When first powered up, \EFI\Boot\ is the folder that the UEFI firmware searches for so it can execute \EFI\Boot\bootx64.efi which then boots the PC. On a plain Windows PC the bootx64.efi file is from Microsoft and points to \EFI\Microsoft\ then Windows boots normally. The Linux install process replaces bootx64.efi with a different bootx64.efi which points to \EFI\debian\ instead. This is also a good time to use Windows to back up the Debian-specific bootx64.efi file. Fortunately, the Mint install process runs a Grub routine including os-prober, which as the name implies, probes for other OS's besides the Linux you are presently installing at the time. And auto-adds any OS's found, to the new Linux multi-boot menu. So it reliably picks up a regular Windows installation and adds an entry for that Windows to the Linux bootmenu. Basically that Windows bootentry points to the same old \EFI\Microsoft\ folder which is unchanged and then boots Windows normally when selected. Unfortunately, os-prober has been commented out of the Grub files and the probe only functions upon OS installation. So when Grub itself is re-installed or updated at a later time, intentionally or not, os-prober no longer runs by default and Windows will be auto-removed from the Linux bootmenu and you wonder where it went. Windows is still there intact regardless and can be recovered by replacing the Linux bootx64.efi with the original Windows bootx64.efi that you backed up earlier. But that would give you no more menu access to Linux. To avoid this deficiency in the default Grub files, in Linux you need to edit the \etc\default\grub file to uncomment (remove the # hashmark from) the GRUB_DISABLE_OS_PROBER=false line. This basically requires using sudo at the Linux command line since otherwise the file is read-only.

A good filesystem permission API could include any of these which would make users WAY safer and enable developers to request far smaller scopes: - Allow the developer to specify the common location(s) that they need access to. Allow an app to read your files but prevent writes or deletes. - Time limited access. Allow some kind of access and allow the user to auto-expire it rather than having to remember it exists. - Allow for negative access (i.e. allow labels or tags on directories to mark them as sensitive and prevent access by default - browsers could do this for their cookie stores, `~/.ssh` could ship with it as a default, etc.) Apple could have used this opportunity to think through the question of "why do developers ask for filesystem access, and how can we allow those various shapes in their narrowest instantiations", but instead they built a bad API that will (I would guess) not actually allow developers to be more judicious or achieve any of the user-safety benefits. > People are playing propaganda games in order to pretend that the copyrights of LLM training material aren't being violated. They're rarely making logical or legal arguments. You have not provided a logical or legal argument for the opposite claim either, and the opposite claim is the one that has the burden of proof in court. In order for LLM training to violate copyright, it needs to fulfill criteria set out by the law that define what constitutes copyright violation. Current copyright law does not mention LLMs directly (unless it's been updated very recently, which I doubt), so a degree of legal interpretation is necessary to determine whether LLM training falls under the law. It is not wrong (nor illogical!) to point out that such an interpretation must be done with care, lest it suddenly imply that human training is also a violation. We can't have that. Actual copyright law will generally say that in order to violate copyright, a work must “substantially resemble” the original in some meaningful way (and also not fall under fair use or some other exception), or a similar phrasing that is the same in spirit. Does an LLM resemble any substantial portions of the works it was trained on? Well, the LLM itself doesn't (it's just a list of weights), but it could be made to reproduce some substantial portions, so you could make an argument similar to your zip file. Such an argument would only apply to situations where you're disseminating the weights, i.e., open weights models. The case of a chat interface that lets you use an LLM with “secret” weights is a whole other issue. Now the LLM itself is no longer relevant, but only its output (as that is what you're disseminating). Here, the big vendors have taken substantial steps to prevent the output of substantial portions of copyrighted material, even erring on the side of false positives (better to refuse than to risk infringement). Now it could easily be argued that the training process is completely irrelevant because it happened entirely in private, and only the output is relevant and must be decided on a case-by-case basis. These are some legal arguments, and as you can see, they do not easily or quickly lead to a clear-cut resolution.
